nodes.title: Security: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Security. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: What type of attack involves flooding a network switch with random MAC addresses?
flashcards.back: MAC flooding attacks overwhelm a switch's CAM (Content Addressable Memory) table. When full, the switch broadcasts all frames, allowing an attacker to capture traffic.

flashcards.front: What is a DMZ in network security?
flashcards.back: A DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) is a network segment that sits between the internet and the internal LAN, hosting publicly accessible servers (web, mail) while protecting the internal network.

flashcards.front: What protocol is used to securely manage network devices over an encrypted conne?
flashcards.back: SSH (Secure Shell) provides encrypted remote access for device management, replacing the insecure Telnet. SSH uses port 22 and provides authentication and encryption.

flashcards.front: What is a Rogue DHCP server attack?
flashcards.back: A rogue DHCP server responds to client requests before the legitimate server, providing a malicious default gateway (attacker's device) to intercept traffic — a man-in-the-middle attack.

nodes.title: Routing: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Routing. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: Which routing protocol uses the Bellman-Ford algorithm?
flashcards.back: RIP (Routing Information Protocol) uses the Bellman-Ford algorithm and hop count as its metric. OSPF uses Dijkstra's SPF algorithm, EIGRP uses DUAL.

flashcards.front: Which protocol provides redundant default gateway capability in a vendor-neutral?
flashcards.back: VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol) is the IEEE standard for default gateway redundancy — vendor neutral. HSRP and GLBP are Cisco-proprietary. All use a virtual IP/MAC shared among routers.

flashcards.front: What is split horizon in distance-vector routing?
flashcards.back: Split horizon prevents routing loops by not advertising routes back the direction they came from. Split horizon with poison reverse sends the route back with infinite metric (poison) instead.

flashcards.front: What is BGP and where is it used?
flashcards.back: BGP (EGP) manages routing between autonomous systems (AS numbers). It's used by ISPs to exchange routes on the internet and by enterprises with multiple ISP connections (multihoming). Path vector protocol.

pairs.stem: Which protocol provides redundant default gateway capability in a vendor-neutral way?
What is a supernet or CIDR block aggregation?

pairs.option: They are identical in all ways

What is a default route and how does it affect routing decisions?
pairs.option: A route for 0.0.0.0/0 — matches any destination not found in the routing table. The 'gateway of last resort'. All unmatched packets follow this route (typically toward an ISP or firewall)

nodes.title: Protocols: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Protocols. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: Which port does SMTP use by default?
flashcards.back: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) uses port 25 for server-to-server email relay. Port 587 is used for authenticated client-to-server submission. Port 110 is POP3, 143 is IMAP.

flashcards.front: What is LLDP and how does it differ from CDP?
flashcards.back: LLDP (IEEE 802.1AB) is the open-standard equivalent of Cisco's CDP. Both advertise device capabilities, port info, and IP addresses at Layer 2. Most modern multi-vendor environments use LLDP.

flashcards.front: What port does RDP use?
flashcards.back: RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) uses TCP/UDP port 3389 for Windows remote desktop connections. Exposing RDP directly to the internet is a major security risk — use VPN or RDP Gateway instead.

flashcards.front: What is ICMP and what is it used for?
flashcards.back: ICMP is used by devices to send error messages and operational info. Ping = ICMP Echo Request/Reply. Traceroute = sends packets with TTL=1,2,3... and collects ICMP Time Exceeded messages from each hop. used for error reporting, diagnostics (ping uses echo request/reply, traceroute uses TTL exceeded messages)

nodes.title: Ethernet: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Ethernet. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between half-duplex and full-duplex Ethernet?
flashcards.back: Modern switched Ethernet uses full-duplex — simultaneous TX/RX, no collisions, no CSMA/CD needed. Half-duplex shares the medium — only one device transmits at a time using CSMA/CD collision avoidance.

flashcards.front: What is flow control in networking?
flashcards.back: Flow control prevents buffer overflow at the receiver. Ethernet uses PAUSE frames (802.3x) in full-duplex. TCP uses its sliding window mechanism for end-to-end flow control.

flashcards.front: What does MTU stand for, and what is the standard Ethernet MTU?
flashcards.back: MTU defines the largest data unit transmitted without fragmentation. Standard Ethernet MTU = 1500 bytes. Jumbo frames (9000 bytes) reduce overhead for large data transfers (storage, HPC). MTU mismatch causes packet drops. 1500 bytes is the standard Ethernet MTU. Jumbo frames extend to 9000 bytes

flashcards.front: What is PoE (Power over Ethernet)?
flashcards.back: PoE (802.3af: 15.4W), PoE+ (802.3at: 30W), and PoE++ (802.3bt: 60-100W) power IP phones, wireless APs, IP cameras, and IoT devices through the network cable — no separate power outlet needed.

pairs.stem: What is the difference between half-duplex and full-duplex Ethernet?
pairs.option: Half-duplex: send OR receive (not simultaneously), used with hubs. Full-duplex: simultaneous send and receive, used with switches. No collisions in full-duplex

pairs.stem: What is PoE (Power over Ethernet)?
pairs.option: Delivers electrical power along with data over standard Ethernet cabling to devices like IP phones, APs, and cameras — eliminating separate power adapters

pairs.stem: What does MTU stand for, and what is the standard Ethernet MTU?
What is flow control in networking?
What is the difference between half-duplex and full-duplex collisions?
pairs.option: Half-duplex: CSMA/CD detects and retransmits after collisions. Full-duplex: no collisions possible (separate TX/RX pairs) — CSMA/CD disabled. Modern switched Ethernet is always full-duplex

nodes.title: Management: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Management. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: What is SNMP and what is it used for?
flashcards.back: SNMP (v1, v2c, v3) allows network management systems (NMS) to poll device stats (CPU, interfaces, errors) and configure devices. SNMPv3 adds encryption and authentication — always use v3 in production. used to monitor and manage network devices by querying and setting device parameters

flashcards.front: What is a network baseline?
flashcards.back: A baseline captures normal performance (bandwidth utilization, latency, error rates, CPU). When issues arise, comparing current metrics against the baseline quickly identifies anomalies.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a network topology diagram?
flashcards.back: Physical topology: actual cable/device layout. Logical topology: how data flows. Network diagrams help technicians understand the network, troubleshoot faster, and plan changes without disruption.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of IPAM in network management?
flashcards.back: IPAM tools (Windows Server IPAM, phpIPAM, Infoblox) provide visibility into IP address utilization, prevent conflicts, manage DHCP scopes, and integrate with DNS. Critical for large networks to avoid IP chaos.

nodes.title: Mixed Topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Mixed Topics. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A network cable test shows a 'split pair' fault. What does this mean?
flashcards.back: A split pair occurs when wires from different twisted pairs are connected together. It passes a continuity test but causes excessive crosstalk and poor performance. causing crosstalk

flashcards.front: What is the maximum cable length for Cat5e/Cat6 UTP in a standard Ethernet run?
flashcards.back: The maximum segment length for 10BASE-T, 100BASE-TX, and 1000BASE-T over UTP (Cat5e/Cat6) is 100 meters (328 feet), including patch cables.

flashcards.front: What is a fiber optic cable and what are its advantages over copper?
flashcards.back: Fiber optic advantages: immune to electromagnetic interference, no ground loops, much longer distances (SMF: up to 80km, MMF: up to 2km), higher bandwidth (100G+ easier than copper), and secure (no signal radiation). immune to EMI, much greater bandwidth (100Gbps+), longer distances (up to 80km single-mode), no electrical hazards

flashcards.front: What is the difference between single-mode and multi-mode fiber?
flashcards.back: SMF: 8-10 micron core, single light path, longer distances, used for WAN/MAN. MMF: 50-62.5 micron core, multiple light paths (modal dispersion limits distance), used for campus/data center LAN (OM1-OM5). longer distance (km), laser source, yellow jacket. Multi-mode (MMF): multiple light paths, shorter distance (up to 2km), LED/VCSEL source, orange/aqua jacket
